paragraphs: Here's the big idea, friend: Paul wasn't running this day, the Lord was. Paul walks in with a clear conscience, gets slapped for it, and then gets a day that only goes downhill. He is struck on the mouth, he fusses at the high priest and has to say he didn't know who the man was (Acts 23:1-5). That's a human day, and it looks a lot like a Monday you'd rather not talk about.

Then Paul sees what the room is made of. The Sadducees and the Pharisees disagree about the resurrection, so he names his hope in it, and the room splits (Acts 23:6-8). Notice what the scribes from the Pharisees say: "We find nothing wrong with this man." (Acts 23:9) Paul's hope in the resurrection wasn't a trick, friend. It was what he truly believed, and he said it out loud when it cost him something. When the room gets so loud that the commander fears they will tear Paul to pieces (Acts 23:10), I think Paul needed more than a plan. He needed a word from the Lord.

And he gets one. "The following night the Lord stood near Paul and said, 'Take courage! As you have testified about Me in Jerusalem, so also you must testify in Rome.'" (Acts 23:11) Nobody in that council gave Paul his next step, and the Lord did. So when your day goes sideways, baker, you don't have to be perfect, and you don't have to have it all figured out. Stay faithful where you stand, and let the Lord keep His word about where you're going. Paul's story is a long way from over, and so is yours.
